title: I built a strategy RPG that Twitch chat plays live — how AI fit into a solo dev pipeline
author: SavingsMaterial3105
selftext:
RaidCast is a fantasy strategy RPG made for streams: viewers type !join in Twitch, Kick or YouTube chat, and their own armies march into the streamer's battle. Between streams each viewer grows their own city, hero and gear.

A bit of background: I'm a streamer myself and I've played strategy games and RPGs for a very long time. I wanted a stream integration that I would actually enjoy using on my own channel, and that longtime fans of the genre would enjoy too. So every feature in the game comes from my own design and preferences, and I control all of the game logic. AI is a tool in that process, not the designer.

Code is writen together with AI coding agents (Claude Code and Codex). What made that work wasn't the model, it was rules. The repo has a written rules file the agents must follow: performance budgets (no extra SQL queries or JSON parsing in normal actions without measuring), "never reset player progress to get around a bug", one documentation file per game module, and deploys only from a clean main branch. Without that, agents happily "fix" things by deleting the hard parts.

The hardest part is the shared battles, where thousands of units fight at once. AI helps a lot with refactoring, but every performance change still gets measured by hand, because a model will confidently tell you something is faster when it isn't.

Art and audio: key art, buldings and many visual assets were generated with AI tools, then picked and fitted into the game by hand. Music and sound effects too.

I've been building RaidCast for a little over two months, testing it every day, fixing logic and adding new features. Right now I'm running stress tests so early access can start smoothly on October 29. And this is just the start: PvP is planned, and PvE will keep growing for players who'd rather not fight other players.

Quetion for other devs here: how do you stop coding agents from drifting over a long project? A rules file worked for me, but I'm curious what others use.
